name: Composition & Biochemistry of Foods

objectives.text: Identify water, carbohydrates, proteins, and fats as the main components that make up foods
Sort common agricultural products such as grain, milk, meat, eggs, and vegetable oil by the main component each contains
Use simple tests such as iodine for starch and brown paper for fat to detect components in food samples
Describe how crops build sugars and starches through photosynthesis and how livestock store proteins and fats in meat, milk, and eggs
Explain how the amount of free water in a food, measured as water activity, determines how quickly the food spoils
Classify food carbohydrates as monosaccharides, disaccharides, or polysaccharides and give an agricultural source of each
Describe how proteins are built from amino acids and identify major food proteins such as casein in milk, gluten in wheat, and myosin in meat
Summarize the chemical structure and properties of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, and minerals as food constituents
Analyze a nutrition facts panel to determine the proportion of carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids in a food product
Distinguish saturated and unsaturated fatty acids by structure and relate each to whether a fat is solid or liquid at room temperature
Explain how starch gelatinization and retrogradation change the texture of grain products during cooking and storage
Explain how protein denaturation, coagulation, gelation, and emulsification give eggs, milk, and meat their functional properties in foods
Compare Maillard browning, caramelization, and enzymatic browning by their reactants, conditions, and effects on food quality
Explain how naturally occurring enzymes drive changes such as fruit ripening, meat tenderization, and cheese ripening
Analyze how postmortem glycolysis, pH decline, and rigor mortis convert muscle to meat and affect carcass quality
Analyze how heat, light, oxygen, and metal ions drive lipid oxidation and rancidity in fats, oils, and meat products
Perform proximate analysis procedures for moisture, ash, fat, and protein on a food sample from an agricultural commodity
Evaluate laboratory results for the water activity and moisture content of a food sample to judge its shelf stability
Analyze how food processors apply biochemistry such as fermentation and enzyme technology to develop value-added food products from raw commodities
Design an experiment that tests how altering a food's water activity changes its microbial stability

changes: Reframed the grade 3 food groups objective and the grade 5 energy objective around food composition, since nutrition belongs to the sibling sub-topic Nutrition & Food Quality. Kept the water activity, nutrition label, lab evaluation, and hypothesis objectives. The hypothesis objective is now an experimental design task. Added a progression of composition competencies: simple tests for components, agricultural origins of constituents, carbohydrate classes, amino acids and food proteins, and fatty acid saturation. Added food biochemistry topics: starch gelatinization, protein functionality, browning reactions, enzymes, postmortem muscle to meat conversion, lipid oxidation, proximate analysis, and biochemistry in value-added processing. Linked these to commodity, SAE, and Food Science CDE contexts. Additives and sensory work were left to the sibling sub-topics.
